passages.t: A queen's coup, and a hidden child
passages.happening:
‘When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she proceeded to annihilate all the royal heirs’ (verse 1).

But Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, takes Ahaziah's infant son Joash and steals him away from among the king's sons who are being killed. She hides him and his nurse in a bedroom, ‘and he was not killed’ (verse 2). ‘And Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD for six years while Athaliah ruled the land’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The alliance between Judah and the house of Ahab, begun under Jehoshaphat and sealed by marriage, now nearly destroys the line of David. While Jehu wipes out Ahab's house in the north, Ahab's daughter seizes power in the south and tries to wipe out David's house. It is one of the moments of greatest danger in the Bible for God's promise to David that his house and throne would endure.

Athaliah reigned about 841 to 835 BC, the only ruler of Judah not of David's line and the only reigning queen in Israel or Judah. She was Ahab's daughter and Omri's granddaughter, and she brought the worship of Baal to Jerusalem as Jezebel had brought it to Samaria. Killing a rival's heirs was a standard way to hold a usurped throne. Her aim was to end the dynasty and rule in her own right.

The counter-move is told as briefly as the crime. A royal infant would have had a nurse, and she was hidden with him. The temple, with its storerooms and chambers, was one of the few places in Jerusalem where a child could be kept out of the palace's sight. Chronicles adds that Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the priest. The word for the royal heirs is zera, seed, the word at the heart of the promises to Abraham and to David. Here that seed is down to one child.
passages.later: The LORD had promised David, ‘Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me’ (2 Samuel 7:16). Moses' mother, too, ‘hid him for three months’ (Exodus 2:2) from a king who was killing boys.
passages.hard:
What should be said about a ruler who killed her own grandchildren?

The text names the crime in a single verse and does not describe it, and these notes do the same. Athaliah set out to kill the royal heirs, who were her own son's children, to take the throne for herself. The chapter does not soften it, and it does not linger on it. It turns at once to the woman who saved one child at the risk of her life.

The story is told from the side of the rescuers. God's promise to David hung on one hidden infant, kept alive by an aunt, a nurse and a priest whose names the text remembers.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jehosheba risked her life to hide a child. Ask what courage ordinary people show in keeping God's purposes alive, often out of sight. And ask who near you needs someone to protect them, and what that might cost.

passages.t: A boy crowned in the temple
passages.happening:
In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada brings the commanders of the guard, the Carites and the royal guard into the house of the LORD. He makes a covenant with them, puts them under oath, and shows them the king's son (verse 4). He sets the guard for the Sabbath so that the units coming on duty and those going off are both in place, surrounding the boy with weapons in hand (verses 5-9). He gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David that were kept in the temple (verse 10).

Then Jehoiada brings out the king's son, puts the crown on him, gives him the Testimony and proclaims him king. They anoint him, the people clap their hands, and they cry, “Long live the king!” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The Carites are usually understood as foreign soldiers serving as a royal bodyguard, perhaps from Caria in southwest Asia Minor, a region known for supplying them. Some connect them with the Cherethites who guarded David. The change of the guard on the Sabbath let Jehoiada have twice the usual number of soldiers present without raising suspicion. Chronicles gives the Levites a larger part in the coup.

The coronation has several parts. The crown marked royal authority. The Testimony, edut, was probably a written copy of the covenant, perhaps the copy of the law Deuteronomy says a king should keep and read, or a royal charter; interpreters are not certain. Either way, it showed that the king rules under God's law, not above it. Anointing set him apart, and the people's acclaim confirmed him.

The chapter moves from death to life and from hiding to revelation. Six years hidden, and the seventh brings him out. Jehoiada's careful instructions slow the pace and build the tension before the scene erupts with noise.
passages.later: Deuteronomy says of a king, ‘When he is seated on his royal throne, he must write for himself a copy of this instruction on a scroll’ (Deuteronomy 17:18). A psalm says, ‘in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter’ (Psalm 27:5).
passages.asks: For six years the rightful king was hidden while a usurper ruled. Ask how this story speaks to times when evil seems in charge and God's purposes seem hidden. And ask what it would mean for you to live under God's law the way the young king was handed it.

passages.t: Treason, a covenant, and a quiet city
passages.happening:
Athaliah hears the noise and goes to the temple. She sees the king standing by the pillar, as was the custom, with officers and trumpeters around him and all the people rejoicing. She tears her clothes and cries out treason (verse 14). Jehoiada orders the commanders to bring her out between the ranks, since he has said that she must not be put to death in the house of the LORD (verse 15). They take her to the horses' entrance to the palace grounds, and she is put to death there (verse 16).

‘Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD’s people’ (verse 17), and another between the king and the people. The people go to the temple of Baal and tear it down, smash its altars and idols, and kill Mattan, the priest of Baal (verse 18). They bring the king down to the palace, and Joash takes his seat on the royal throne (verse 19). ‘And all the people of the land rejoiced. And the city was quiet’ (verse 20). Joash is seven years old (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The king stood by the pillar according to custom, a fixed place in the temple court for royal ceremonies; Josiah will stand there too. Her cry of treason is bitterly ironic, since her own reign began with treason and murder.

The chapter ends with two covenants, the destruction of Baal's temple in Jerusalem, and a quiet city, in pointed contrast to the bloodshed of Jehu's purge in the chapter before. Restoring a king of David's line goes with renewing the whole people's covenant with God. Joash, also spelled Jehoash, began to reign about 835 BC.
passages.later: Chronicles tells the same coronation and covenant, and names the princess Jehoshabeath, ‘the wife of Jehoiada the priest’ (2 Chronicles 22:11).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take Athaliah's death and the killing of Mattan?

The text tells both in single verses and does not dwell on them. Athaliah had seized the throne by murdering the royal heirs, and her death ends a usurper's reign; Jehoiada takes care that she is not killed in the LORD's house. Mattan was the priest of the temple of Baal that Athaliah had brought to Jerusalem.

The chapter's own emphasis falls elsewhere: on a covenant renewed and a city at peace. Nothing here gives anyone today a warrant to overthrow a ruler by force in God's name, or to harm anyone over religion. The New Testament gives the church no sword in matters of worship.
passages.asks: Jehoiada's reform began with a covenant to be the LORD's people. Ask what the difference is between changing leaders and renewing a people's commitment to God. And ask what would make your own household, or your church, a quiet city.
